profile.reading:
This Lumen colocation facility is located at 870 Duane Avenue, Santa Clara, CA 95054, per public property records; Lumen does not publish individual building addresses or specs on its own site for any of its 175-plus North American colocation sites. Lumen Technologies, formerly CenturyLink (renamed Lumen on September 14, 2020, with its stock ticker changing from CTL to LUMN on September 18, 2020) and built in part on CenturyLink's November 1, 2017 acquisition of Level 3 Communications, operates this facility as part of a network-centric edge colocation product rather than a wholesale hyperscale campus. Lumen's own colocation data sheet states more than 175 carrier-neutral data centers across more than 60 North American markets, offering cabinet power in the 3 to 15 kilowatt range described as varying by site; unlike the wholesale operators tracked elsewhere in this registry, Lumen does not disclose per-building square footage or total MW capacity for any of its sites, treating those specifications as commercially site-dependent rather than public data.

California regulators are actively reworking how large data center loads are billed and interconnected as demand grows statewide, directly relevant to Santa Clara's dense colocation submarket. Under SB 57 (2025), the California Public Utilities Commission opened a rate-design rulemaking in April 2026 specifically addressing electric rate impacts of data centers and other large transmission-connected loads, expected to run roughly two years and examine dedicated data-center tariffs and the risk of costs shifting onto residential and small-business ratepayers. The California Independent System Operator separately published a formal issue paper on large-load interconnection considerations in January 2026, part of an ongoing CAISO regulatory track addressing how data centers connect to the state's transmission grid.

reading.body:
This Lumen facility sits in Santa Clara County as a carrier-neutral colocation site rather than a wholesale hyperscale campus. Lumen does not publish power capacity, square footage, or per-building specifications for any of its 175-plus North American colocation sites, treating those figures as commercially confidential and site-dependent. The operator's public data sheet describes cabinet power ranging from 3 to 15 kilowatts per site, which differs structurally from the tens to hundreds of megawatts disclosed by hyperscale operators building dedicated AI campuses.

California's utility and grid regulators have opened formal proceedings that directly affect colocation facilities in this market. The California Public Utilities Commission began a rate-design rulemaking in April 2026 specifically examining electric rates for data centers and the risk of cost-shifting to residential ratepayers, expected to run roughly two years. The California Independent System Operator published a separate issue paper in January 2026 on how large loads interconnect to the state's transmission grid, part of an ongoing regulatory track that will reshape how data center demand connects to the system.

Without published capacity figures, this facility cannot be ranked against California's disclosed hyperscale capacity. Of 103 mapped facilities in California, only 11 publish megawatt figures, totaling 365 MW statewide. This site's rank of 12 reflects the state registry's methodology rather than a disclosed capacity claim, and should be read as a gap: colocation operators control an unknown share of the state's data center load, and that load is now subject to regulatory redesign in real time.
